newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Crown jeweller looks to Russia's new tsars.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Crown jeweller looks to Russia's new tsars.

text.p: Christian Bolin is nostalgic for the days when Tsarina Alexandra Feodorovna could suddenly decide she needed a new tiara. The Russian court used to be his firm's biggest customer.
In 1900 the Tsarina's rush order for a tiara set with 100 carats of Colombian emeralds and 225 carats of South African diamonds -- plus a necklace and a stomacher -- was all in a day's work.

These days, with royals across Europe under pressure to keep down spending, business is a lot slower for his Swedish family firm, W.A. Bolin, which specialises in customised opulent jewels and silver for the seriously wealthy.

With Sweden's royals better known for riding bicycles than sporting gaudy gems, the Stockholm jeweller is again pinning its hopes on a new generation of Russian rich, hoping to return to the country where his family first found fortune.
"It would be fantastic," says Bolin, whose sights are set on the country's new capitalists.
"Russians are lavish," he says. "They like big patterns. I think the children of those who are rich now will grow into sophisticated bourgeois."
CALAMITIES AND CLOSE SHAVES CHEQUER FIRM'S PAST

Originally a seafaring family, piloted by calamity to St Petersburg in 1831 after a ship carrying their livelihood went down in a storm, the Bolins became crown jewellers to the empire until the 1917 revolution.

The Bolin name may be less well known than their St Petersburg rivals Faberge, but they made gem-studded brooches, necklaces, cigarette boxes and other trinkets which stylish Russians casually flaunted in high-society circles.
Faberge was put out of business by the revolution, but the Bolin firm survived through a stroke of luck. In 1912 they had moved much of their stock to Germany to set up a new branch.

When Germany declared war on Russia, the Bolins fled to Sweden with the jewels and silver and opened up shop in Stockholm, a year before the Bolsheviks took power and confiscated all their Russian assets.
SILVER ASPARAGUS HOLDER ON SHOW
For a short time, until January 12, some of the house of Bolin's most spectacular pieces are on show at Stockholm's Armoury Museum to mark the firm's 200-year jubilee.

A diamond brooch with pictures of Tsar Alexander III and Tsarina Maria Feodorovna, and another with a sparkling star sapphire wreathed in diamonds are among the 300 pieces that Bolin scoured museums and dank Moscow antique stores to find.

There is a silver holder especially for asparagus; a flower pendant with petals of diamonds, rubies and sapphires and leaves in pure gold; a necklace that looks like lace but is crafted of tiny oriental pearls strung with gold.
REBUILDING LINKS WITH RUSSIA

But with a history of near-catastrophes for his business, Bolin is not going to rush into Russia's fast-changing business world -- despite the fact that a building bearing the family name still stands in St Petersburg.
"People tell me I should be in a hurry to be the first to set up in Russia, but I don't think that is very wise," he said. "I'll see what I can do."

He has already revived a small link with Russia, commissioning a Russian goldsmith to make tiny bright egg-shaped pendants from gold, enamel on silver and diamond. Complete in a small birch box, their prices range from $200-$4,400.

The grandeur of past orders may be gone for ever. Modern customers often demand that Bolin keep materials costs within a budget. Swedes, who with their Calvinist roots tend to dislike ostentation, want simpler lines and moderate prices.
"Now the bigger part of the price is the work, not the materials," Bolin said. "Before it was the other way around."
Even the Swedish royal family are not very interested: "They don't seem so keen on it," Bolin said. "They own a lot of jewellery already."
